steps.head: Common denominator
steps.text: Find a number both bottoms divide into. The smallest one keeps the numbers small.

steps.head: Convert
steps.text: Rewrite each fraction with that bottom. Whatever you multiply the bottom by, multiply the top by too.

steps.head: Add the tops
steps.text: Add the numerators. The denominator stays the same.

steps.head: Simplify
steps.text: If the top and bottom share a factor, divide both by it.

parts.title: Explain
parts.blurb: Why you can't just add the tops and bottoms — and what to do instead.
parts.say: Hey, I'm Pip. In about ten minutes you'll be able to add any two fractions, even when the bottoms don't match.

steps.say: Before I explain anything — have a guess. Wrong guesses are useful, so don't overthink it.

g.say: Spot on. Now let's see *why* it's {5/6}, so you can do it every time.
That's the most common guess — you added the tops and added the bottoms. It feels right, but it isn't. Let's see why.
Not quite, but you've got something to compare against. Let's work out the real answer.

skip.label: Not sure
skip.say: Fair enough. Let's work it out together.

screens.say: Here are {1/2} and {1/3} as bars. The pieces are different sizes — halves are bigger than thirds — so you can't just count them up.
And that popular guess, {2/5}? It's *smaller* than {1/2} on its own. Adding more to {1/2} can't make it shrink, so adding tops and bottoms never works.
The fix: cut both into pieces of the **same size**. Sixths work for both. {1/2} is the same as {3/6}, and {1/3} is the same as {2/6}.
Now the pieces match, so just count them: 3 sixths + 2 sixths = 5 sixths. So {1/2} + {1/3} = {5/6}.
That's the whole method. Four steps. The bottom number is the **denominator**, the top is the **numerator**.

parts.title: Watch
parts.blurb: A worked example, one line at a time.
parts.say: Watch me do one. Tap **Next line** when you're ready for the next bit — you can go back any time.

lines.say: Here's {3/10} + {1/6}. The bottoms are 10 and 6 — different-sized pieces. So step 1: find a common denominator.
List the multiples of each bottom until they share one. Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30…
…and of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. First match: **30**. (10 × 6 = 60 would work too — it just gives bigger numbers.)
Convert. 10 × 3 = 30, so multiply the top by 3 too: {3/10} = {9/30}. And 6 × 5 = 30, so {1/6} = {5/30}.
Same-size pieces now, so add the tops: 9 + 5 = 14. The bottom stays 30 — adding pieces doesn't change their size.
Simplify. 14 and 30 are both even, so divide both by 2: {7/15}. 7 and 15 share no other factor, so that's as simple as it gets.

screens.outro: So {3/10} + {1/6} = {7/15}. Next, you do one — I'll be right here.

parts.title: Try one together
parts.blurb: You type each line. I'll check it as you go.
parts.say: Your turn. You type each line, I'll check it. Use the keypad — tap a box to choose where your number goes.

screens.outro: {1/4} + {5/12} = {2/3}. That's the whole method, done by you.

steps.say: First: what's the smallest number that both 4 and 12 divide into?

n.say: Looks like you added 4 and 12. We need a number they both divide into exactly — and 12 doesn't go into 16.
4 goes into 4, but 12 doesn't. The number has to work for both bottoms.
That works — both divide into it. But 12 is smaller (4 already goes into 12), so we'll use 12 to keep the numbers small.
Check it: does 4 go into it exactly? Does 12? It needs both.

steps.correct: Yes — 12. Since 4 goes into 12, the bigger denominator already does the job.
hints: Count up in 4s: 4, 8, 12… Stop at the first one that 12 also divides into.
steps.why: A common denominator lets us cut both fractions into same-size pieces. Any common multiple works; the smallest keeps the numbers easy.

steps.say: Now rewrite both fractions as twelfths. Whatever you multiply the bottom by, do the same to the top.

a.say: You changed the bottom of {1/4} to 12 but left the top as 1. 4 × 3 = 12, so the top needs × 3 as well.
Your first fraction is equal to {1/4}, which is good — but it needs 12 on the bottom so the pieces match.
First fraction: the bottom's right. 4 was multiplied by 3 to get 12, so multiply the top, 1, by 3.
{1/4} needs to become something over 12. What do you multiply 4 by to get 12?

b.say: Your second fraction equals {5/12}, but keep it in twelfths so both fractions match.
{5/12} already has 12 on the bottom, so it doesn't need to change.

steps.correct: Yes, that's right. {1/4} = {3/12}, and {5/12} was already in twelfths.
hints: Start with {1/4}. What times 4 gives 12? Do the same to the top.
4 × 3 = 12, so 1 × 3 = 3. The second fraction already has 12 on the bottom.
steps.why: Multiplying the top and bottom by the same number is like multiplying by 1: the value stays the same, only the size of the pieces changes.

steps.say: The pieces match now. Add the tops. What happens to the bottom?

s.say: You added the bottoms too. The pieces are still twelfths — putting them together doesn't make them smaller. Keep 12.
Yes — and you've simplified already. {8/12} = {2/3}, so that's the final answer.
That's equal to {8/12} — you've started simplifying. Let's write {8/12} here and finish simplifying on the next line.
The bottom's right. Now add the tops: 3 + 5.
Add just the tops, 3 + 5, and keep the bottom as 12.

hints: Only the tops get added. The bottom stays 12.
steps.why: 3 twelfths plus 5 twelfths is 8 twelfths — the same way 3 apples plus 5 apples is 8 apples. The 'twelfths' is the unit.

steps.say: Last step: can {8/12} be simplified? Look for a number that divides into both 8 and 12.

f.say: That's where we started. 8 and 12 are both in the 4 times table — divide both by 4.
Nearly — that's equal, but the top and bottom still share a factor. Divide again.
That isn't equal to {8/12}. Divide the top and the bottom by the *same* number.

steps.correct: Yes, that's right. 8 and 12 both divide by 4, giving {2/3}.
hints: Both 8 and 12 are in the 4 times table.
steps.why: Dividing the top and bottom by the same number keeps the value the same. Use the biggest shared factor to get there in one go.

parts.title: On your own
parts.blurb: A new one. Same steps, less chat from me.
parts.say: This one's yours. I'll stay quiet unless you ask for a hint.

screens.outro: {7/10} + {2/15} = {5/6}. You did that on your own.

n.say: That's 10 + 15. We need a number both 10 and 15 divide into exactly.
That works. 30 is the smallest one, though, so we'll use 30 to keep the numbers small.
Does 10 go into it exactly? Does 15? It needs both.

hints: Count up in 15s: 15, 30, 45… Which is the first one 10 also divides into?
steps.why: 30 is the smallest number in both the 10 and 15 times tables. 10 × 15 = 150 also works, but the numbers get big.

a.say: First fraction: the bottom's right, but the top needs the same × 3.
First fraction: equal to {7/10}, but it needs 30 on the bottom.
First fraction: 10 × 3 = 30, so the top is 7 × 3.
First fraction: what do you multiply 10 by to get 30? Do that to the top too.

b.say: Second fraction: 15 × 2 = 30, so double the top as well.
Second fraction: equal to {2/15}, but it needs 30 on the bottom.
Second fraction: 15 × 2 = 30, so the top is 2 × 2.
Second fraction: what do you multiply 15 by to get 30? Do that to the top too.

hints: 10 × 3 = 30 and 15 × 2 = 30. Do the same to each top.
steps.why: Multiplying the top and bottom by the same number doesn't change the value — it just cuts the pieces smaller.

s.say: Careful — only the tops get added. The bottom stays 30.
Yes — and you've simplified already: {25/30} = {5/6}. That's the final answer.
That's equal to {25/30} — you've started simplifying. Let's write {25/30} here and finish on the next line.
Add the tops, 21 + 4, and keep the bottom as 30.

hints: Add the tops. The bottom stays 30.

f.say: Can it go further? 25 and 30 are both in the 5 times table.
Equal, but not fully simplified yet — the top and bottom still share a factor.
That isn't equal to {25/30}. Divide the top and bottom by the same number.

steps.correct: Yes, that's right. 25 and 30 both divide by 5, giving {5/6}.
hints: 25 and 30 are both in the 5 times table.
steps.why: 5 and 6 share no factor except 1, so {5/6} is in its simplest form.

end.title: You can add fractions now.
end.say: That's it. Any two fractions, same four steps. Nice work.
